title: Fertilizer Crisis: How the Iran War Is Squeezing U.S. Farmers—and What It Means for Your Food
summary: When the U.S. and Israel went to war with Iran, oil prices grabbed headlines. But another critical commodity has been quietly choking global supply chains: fertilizer. Before the conflict, roughly one-third of the world's seaborne fertilizer passed through the Strait of Hormuz, according to UN Trade and Development. With that chokepoint now closed, shipments from the Persian Gulf have plummeted, and prices have soared. The ripple effects are hitting American farmers hard. Fertilizer is a major expense—corn and wheat producers can spend around a third of their operating costs on it. A survey by the National Corn Growers Association found that half of responding farmers won't apply the full amount of fertilizer to their corn crop this year, largely due to higher costs and limited availability. Some are switching to soybeans, which require less nitrogen. The USDA predicts corn acreage will drop from 98.8 million last year to 95.3 million, while soybean acreage rises from 81.2 million to 85.4 million. But will this mean sticker shock at the supermarket? Probably not. Agricultural economists say the fertilizer shortage alone is unlikely to cause a major spike in retail food prices. 'Very little of that is going to be directly attributable to fertilizer,' said Chris Barrett, a professor at Cornell University. That's because fertilizer is just one small slice of the food dollar. According to the USDA, only about 12 cents of every dollar consumers spend on food goes to the farm; the rest covers transportation, processing, wholesaling, and retail. And fertilizer accounts for just 7% of farm budgets on average. Farmers are in a tough spot. They face higher input costs but have little bargaining power to raise crop prices. 'Those buyers will go to other farmers to try and get it cheaper,' said Rob Vos of the International Food Policy Research Institute. Still, the fertilizer crunch is part of a 'really unpleasant layer cake' of pressures, Barrett said, including tariffs, extreme weather, and high fuel and labor costs. Together, they could nudge food inflation up by 0.1 to 0.5 percentage points in 2027, according to a TD Economics analysis. The bigger worry? Farmers are twice as concerned about the 2027 crop as this year's—suggesting the pain may just be beginning.
why_it_matters: This story connects a war thousands of miles away to the food on your table: it reveals how tightly the world’s supply chains are linked and how a single chokepoint can raise costs for farmers, eventually affecting grocery bills.

keywords.explanation: A commodity is a basic raw material or product, like oil, grain, or fertilizer, that can be bought and sold.
A chokepoint is a narrow passage, like a strait or canal, where shipping can easily be blocked, causing big supply problems.
Plummeted means fell extremely quickly and steeply, like a stone dropping from a cliff.
Soared means rose very fast and very high, like a bird shooting up into the sky.
Acreage means the amount of land measured in acres, used here to describe how much farmers are planting.
Input costs are the expenses a farmer pays for things like seeds, fertilizer, and fuel before they can grow and sell a crop.

questions.question: Which waterway, closed by the war, used to carry about one-third of the world's seaborne fertilizer?
About what fraction of their operating costs do corn and wheat farmers usually spend on fertilizer?
Which crop are some farmers switching to because it needs less nitrogen fertilizer?
According to the USDA, about how many cents of every dollar consumers spend on food actually go to the farm?
By how much might food inflation increase in 2027 due to the fertilizer crisis, according to TD Economics?
Which future crop are farmers more worried about than the current one?

background_read: Fertilizers provide key nutrients like nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium that crops need to grow; without them, yields would drop sharply, threatening food supplies.
The Strait of Hormuz is a 21-mile-wide waterway between Iran and Oman—one of the most critical chokepoints in the world because a huge share of global oil and commodities move through it.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) is the federal agency that tracks crop statistics, supports farmers, and analyzes the nation’s food system.
The recent U.S.-Israeli war with Iran disrupted not just oil but also shipments of phosphate and potash from Persian Gulf countries, making fertilizer scarce and expensive worldwide.

Past supply shocks, like the energy crisis of the 1970s or Russia’s war in Ukraine, have shown that when fertilizer prices spike, farmers often apply less, which eventually reduces harvests—but it takes months or years for that to hit supermarket prices.

perspectives.description: The shock could speed up investment in domestic fertilizer production and precision farming techniques, making the U.S. food system less dependent on unstable regions in the future.

Farmers are caught in a squeeze: they must pay much more for fertilizer without being able to charge much more for their crops. Small farms especially could face serious financial trouble, reducing the diversity of food producers.

This crisis highlights how fertilizer is just one layer in a 'layer cake' of pressures—tariffs, extreme weather, and high fuel costs all pile up, showing that food inflation is driven by multiple, interconnected forces.

Policymakers may consider strategic fertilizer reserves or new shipping insurance arrangements for the Strait of Hormuz, while consumers might see small, persistent price increases that could change what people buy and eat in the late 2020s.
